question.leadin: This man was captured at Cajamarca by conquistadors and ransomed for rooms of gold and silver, but the Spanish killed him anyway.
question.text: Name this son of Huayna Capac, who fought his brother Huascar for control of a South American empire.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.leadin: These people stored numerical information by using colored and knotted strings called quipus (KEE-poos).
swap.text: Name these people who also communicated using an extensive road network in the Andes called the "royal road" in Quechua (KEH-choo-uh). Their empire included sites like Machu Picchu (MAH-choo PEEK-choo) in modern-day Peru.
swap.clue: The language Quechua was spoken by members of this empire.

question.text: Identify the Spaniard who conquered the Incan Empire.
question.clue: This man received help from longtime partner Diego Almagro, but he was killed by Almagro's forces in the Battle of Las Salinas.

swap.text: Alongside Bernardo O'Higgins, de San Martin fought for the independence of this future nation. The Battle of Junin was part of this country's war of independence.
swap.clue: That culture in this country was also responsible for creating a series of images called Lines near Palpa that are well-known geoglyphs.

question.text: Paul Kosok discovered the Hummingbird, an earthwork built by these people indigenous to Peru. These people built the city of Cahuachi [ca-WA-chee] and used puquios to irrigate their crops.
question.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

swap.leadin: This term was originally used to describe the zipa chief of the Muisca people who would cover himself in gold and dive into Lake Guatavita.
swap.text: Name this term that was eventually used to describe an empire of gold sought by conquistadors.
swap.clue: During the first part of the journey in which Orellana travelled the length of the Amazon, a valley of Cinnamon and this place were the targets of Gonzalo Pizzaro.

question.text: The mita was used by Spanish rulers to obtain a labor force for this largest silver mine in the Spanish Empire, in which thousands died from mercury poisoning. It lies in present-day Bolivia.
question.clue: Workers in this city still give offerings to a goat-headed underworld deity called "The Uncle" or El Tio.

swap.text: After sacking Ankara in Turkey, Tamerlane allegedly made a pyramid of these objects.
swap.clue: Timur allegedly built pyramids out of these body parts, the protective structure for the brain, which would terrify his enemies.

question.leadin: In the 1860s, ships from this country sailed to Polynesia to abduct laborers through a practice known as "blackbirding"
question.text: Name this country that needed workers for its profitable guano mines. A president of Japanese ancestry fought against the Shining Path in this country.
question.clue: This nation fought its northern neighbor in the Cenepa War.

swap.leadin: The execution of Antonio de Arriaga instigated a rebellion led by a man with this regnal name.
swap.text: Give this two-word name of an indigenous Peruvian rebel leader who claimed descent from the final Sapa Inca. That Neo-Incan ruler with this regnal name was executed by the Spanish in 1572.
swap.clue: The legitimate son of Manco Capac, he was captured an executed for the death of Friar Diego Ortiz.

question.text: Incan relay messengers, the chasquis, carried messages via these "talking knots" that were made of llama hair.
question.clue: This objects that were used for record-keeping and other purposes by the Inca.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the fall of the Inca Empire.
swap.text: This conquistador and 180 men conquered the Inca Empire.
swap.clue: This leader of the "famous thirteen" ambushed a certain opponent at Cajamarca and retrieved twenty-four tons of gold and silver after ordering a room to be filled with precious metal.

question.leadin: Part of these people's confederation was ruled by a zipa, who would cover his body in gold dust and jump into Lake Guatavita along with some gold offerings.
question.text: Name these people, whose confederation was ruled by a zipa in the south and a zaque in the north. The last powerful cacique of these people, Tundama, was killed with a large hammer by Balthasar Maldonado.
question.clue: This confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.

swap.text: Evidence of geoglyphs suggested that the Amazon and Peru may have been home to powerful pre-Columbian civilizations. This Peruvian culture created geoglyphs in the desert that resemble spiders and hummingbirds.
swap.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

question.leadin: According to one crackpot theory, these structures were built using medieval hot-air balloons.
question.text: Name these massive desert drawings that have been hypothesized to represent constellations. Greenpeace activists managed to damage one shaped like a hummingbird in late 2014.
question.answerHtml: Nazca Lines [accept Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa, accept Lineas de Nazca]
question.clue: These things were damaged by Greenpeace activists wearing improper footwear as part of a 2014 protest.

swap.text: This emperor was responsible for the greatest period of Inca expansion. Though the Inca controlled little more than the valley of Cuzco upon his ascent in 1438, due to a series of successful campaigns his dominion extended from Ecuador to northern Chile and Argentina by the time of his death.
swap.clue: This ruler, who legendarily subjugated the (+) Chanka people with stone warriors, organized his realm into four suyus.

question.leadin: After Pizarro's conquests, this system was initially replaced with the encomienda system typical in the rest of the Spanish Americas.
question.text: Name this Inca system under which all able-bodied men from age 15 to 50 were mandated to work on government projects, often for more than 100 days per year.
question.clue: A revival of this system that ignored traditional boundaries was created by Francisco de Toledo to support the new mining town of Huancavelica.

swap.text: The Inca used mit'a ("MITT-ah") labor to construct the rope bridges which connected sections of this 25,000-mile-long system together.
swap.clue: Stations called tambos could be found along this system, which was known in one language as Qhapaq Nan.

question.leadin: Richard MacNeish used this term to name an archaeological phase that includes Cob Swamp in Belize.
question.text: Give this name of a period in which earthquake-resistant nettings called shicras were developed. Caral and Kotosh date from a period of the Andean Late Archaic of this name, which indicates the absence of a technology later perfected by the Moche.

swap.leadin: The Met holds a work made of this material with French lettering and scenes from Greek mythology, and a lliklla ("LEEK-l'yah") made of this material that imitates Spanish-style lattice motifs.
swap.text: Name this material used to make low-quality awasqa or high-quality qunpi ("COMB-pee"), decorated with tukapu motifs. A red llawt'u ("l'YAO-too") decorated the maskhaypacha, an imperial symbol made of this material.
swap.answerHtml: camelid wool [or millma or millwa or willma; accept camelid hair or camelid fur; accept fleece in place of “wool”; accept llama, alpaca, or vicuña in place of “camelid”; prompt on hair or fur; prompt on textile or fabric or clothing or p’achakuna by asking “made of what substance?”; prompt on cotton or utkhu by asking “what material is more commonly used?”; reject “rope” or “chord”]
